lessonTitle: Ischaemic Heart Disease: Atherosclerosis, Angina and Myocardial Infarction

blocks.text: A 58-year-old man is shovelling snow when a heavy, crushing pain builds behind his sternum and spreads to his jaw. He sits down, sweating and nauseated, and the pain does not ease. Forty minutes later in the emergency department his ECG shows ST-segment elevation and his troponin is rising. The same coronary disease that caused years of exertional discomfort has now abruptly blocked an artery.

blocks.markdown: **Ischaemic heart disease (IHD)** is myocardial injury or dysfunction caused by an imbalance between oxygen supply and demand, almost always because of narrowed coronary arteries. The heart extracts about 70% of the oxygen delivered at rest, so it cannot compensate for reduced supply by extracting more; it can only increase flow. Coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole, so perfusion pressure is the aortic diastolic pressure minus the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP).

blocks.caption: Coronary perfusion pressure (mmHg). It falls with low diastolic pressure or a high ventricular filling pressure.
Resistance R of a vessel segment rises with the fourth power of falling radius r, so modest luminal narrowing sharply limits flow.

blocks.title: Perfusion pressure in a failing, hypotensive patient
blocks.prompt: A patient has aortic diastolic pressure 70 mmHg and LVEDP 20 mmHg. Calculate the coronary perfusion pressure, and explain what happens if aortic diastolic pressure falls to 55 mmHg.

steps.text: Perfusion pressure = diastolic pressure - LVEDP = 70 - 20 = 50 mmHg.
If diastolic pressure falls to 55 mmHg while LVEDP is unchanged, perfusion pressure = 55 - 20 = 35 mmHg, a 30% reduction.
A stenotic artery already limits flow, so any fall in perfusion pressure reduces supply below demand in the territory beyond the narrowing, and ischaemia appears.

blocks.answer: Coronary perfusion pressure falls from 50 to 35 mmHg, which can tip a stenosed vascular bed into ischaemia.

blocks.markdown:
### Pathogenesis of an atherosclerotic plaque

Atherosclerosis begins with **endothelial dysfunction** at sites of disturbed flow (arterial branch points), driven by smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and diabetes. Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) enters the intima and is oxidised. Monocytes adhere, migrate in and become macrophages that engulf oxidised LDL to form **foam cells**; clusters form the **fatty streak**. Smooth muscle cells migrate from the media, proliferate and lay down collagen, building a **fibrous cap** over a **necrotic lipid core**. The plaque grows outward at first and then encroaches on the lumen.

blocks.title: Vulnerable plaque and plaque rupture
blocks.text: A vulnerable plaque has a large lipid core, a thin fibrous cap and many inflammatory cells. Macrophage enzymes degrade the cap, and haemodynamic stress can cause it to rupture. Exposure of thrombogenic core material triggers platelet adhesion and clot formation, which may suddenly occlude the lumen. It is rupture with thrombosis, not simply the size of the plaque, that causes acute coronary syndromes.

rows: Fixed stenosis; demand exceeds supply on exertion
Central chest tightness on effort, relieved by rest or nitrate within minutes
Usually normal at rest; transient ST depression during effort
May show ST depression or T-wave change, or be normal
Partial or transient occlusion causing subendocardial necrosis
ST depression or T inversion, no persistent ST elevation
Persistent ST elevation (or new left bundle branch block)

blocks.markdown:
### Troponin and the ECG

**Cardiac troponins (cTnI, cTnT)** are regulatory proteins of the thin filament that leak from necrotic myocytes. They are highly specific for myocardial injury, begin to rise about 3-6 hours after onset (earlier with high-sensitivity assays), peak at about a day and remain elevated for 7-14 days. A rise proves **myocardial injury** but not its cause: sepsis, pulmonary embolism, renal failure and myocarditis can also raise it, so interpretation requires the clinical picture and a rising or falling pattern. **ST elevation** reflects transmural injury, usually from complete occlusion, and is localised by the leads involved.

rows: Right coronary artery (RCA) in most people
blocks.caption: Localisation of STEMI

blocks.title: Interpreting chest pain, ECG and troponin
blocks.prompt: A 64-year-old woman has 25 minutes of rest chest pain. Her ECG shows 2 mm ST depression in V4-V6. Troponin is raised on two samples 3 hours apart, with a rising trend. Classify the syndrome.

steps.text: A raised, rising troponin means myocyte necrosis has occurred, so this is not unstable angina.
No persistent ST elevation means the occlusion is not complete and transmural, so it is not STEMI.
Combine: acute coronary syndrome with myocardial necrosis but without ST elevation.

items: Atherosclerosis risk factors: age, male sex, smoking, hypertension, raised LDL cholesterol, diabetes and family history.
Stable angina: predictable, effort-related, relieved by rest; fixed stenosis, no necrosis.
Unstable angina: crescendo or rest pain, troponin negative.
Infarction: troponin positive; STEMI versus NSTEMI is decided by the ECG.
Complications of infarction include arrhythmia, pump failure, rupture of wall, septum or papillary muscle, and pericarditis.

blocks.title: Normal early troponin does not exclude infarction
blocks.text: Troponin lags the onset of necrosis. A patient with typical pain and ST elevation is treated as STEMI without waiting for a troponin result; patients with suspected NSTEMI need serial testing.

points: Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction and LDL entry, progresses through foam cells and fatty streak to a fibrous-capped plaque, and causes acute events when a vulnerable plaque ruptures and thrombus forms.
Stable angina reflects a fixed stenosis, unstable angina a non-occlusive thrombus without necrosis, and infarction necrosis; troponin separates the last from the first two.
A raised troponin indicates myocardial injury, while ST elevation indicates transmural ischaemia and localises the occluded artery.

questions.stem: Which event is generally considered the initiating step in atherogenesis?

options.text: Endothelial dysfunction with LDL entry into the intima
Formation of the necrotic lipid core

questions.correctOptionText: Endothelial dysfunction with LDL entry into the intima

distractorRationale.a: Correct: injury or dysfunction of the endothelium lets LDL enter the intima and become oxidised, starting the sequence.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: cap rupture is a late complication, not the initiating event.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: calcification occurs later in established plaques.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the lipid core forms after foam cells accumulate and die.

questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis starts when disturbed flow, smoking, hypertension or hyperlipidaemia damage the endothelium and permit LDL to enter the intima. Foam cells, fatty streaks, fibrous cap and lipid core follow in sequence.

questions.stem: Which plaque features most strongly predict rupture and acute thrombosis?

options.text: A large lipid core, thin fibrous cap and abundant macrophages
A small lipid core and thick collagen-rich cap
A purely fatty streak confined to the intima

questions.correctOptionText: A large lipid core, thin fibrous cap and abundant macrophages

distractorRationale.a: Correct: macrophages degrade the cap, leaving a thin shell over a thrombogenic core.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a thick, collagen-rich cap is stable.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: heavily calcified plaques tend to be stable and are less likely to rupture.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: fatty streaks are early, reversible lesions without a cap.

questions.explanation: A thin fibrous cap over a large lipid core and inflamed with macrophages is mechanically weak and prone to rupture. When it ruptures, thrombogenic core contents are exposed to blood and clot forms within minutes.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man gets central chest tightness whenever he climbs two flights of stairs. It settles within about 3 minutes of stopping, and his resting ECG is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: predictable, effort-related pain relieved quickly by rest suggests a fixed stenosis.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: STEMI causes prolonged pain with ST elevation and does not settle in minutes.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: unstable angina involves rest, new-onset or crescendo pain.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: pericarditis is typically pleuritic and positional, not exertional.

questions.explanation: A fixed coronary stenosis restricts flow so that demand outstrips supply only when effort increases oxygen consumption. Rest restores balance and the pain resolves within minutes without myocyte necrosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has 20 minutes of chest pain at rest. His ECG shows transient ST depression that resolves, and serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements over 6 hours remain within the reference range. Which diagnosis fits best?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: rest pain with ischaemic ECG change but no biomarker evidence of necrosis is unstable angina.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: NSTEMI requires a raised troponin.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: STEMI needs persistent ST elevation.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: stable angina is exertional and predictable, not rest pain.

questions.explanation: The discriminator between unstable angina and NSTEMI is myocyte necrosis, which is shown by a troponin rise. Pain at rest indicates a non-occlusive thrombus on a ruptured plaque, which has produced ischaemia but no detectable infarction.

questions.stem: A patient with acute chest pain has ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which coronary artery is most commonly responsible?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: inferior leads usually reflect right coronary territory in right-dominant circulations.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: LAD occlusion produces anterior ST elevation in V1-V4.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: left main occlusion gives extensive anterior and lateral changes, not isolated inferior elevation.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the circumflex mainly supplies the lateral wall, and supplies the inferior wall only in left-dominant systems.

questions.explanation: Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall, which is supplied by the right coronary artery in most people. A circumflex supply is the alternative in left-dominant systems.

questions.stem: A patient with a poor cardiac output has an aortic diastolic pressure of 62 mmHg and a left ventricular end-diastolic pressure of 18 mmHg. Using the approximation in the lesson, calculate the coronary perfusion pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Coronary perfusion pressure is the aortic diastolic pressure minus the LVEDP, so 62 - 18 = 44 mmHg. A raised LVEDP lowers perfusion pressure, which is one reason failing ventricles are vulnerable to subendocardial ischaemia.

questions.stem: A coronary segment has its luminal diameter reduced from 3.0 mm to 1.5 mm by plaque. Assuming resistance is proportional to 1/r^4, by what factor does the resistance of that segment increase? Give a dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: Halving the diameter halves the radius, so resistance scales as 1/(0.5)^4 = 16. Because of this fourth-power dependence, even moderate luminal narrowing sharply limits flow when demand rises.

questions.stem: Describe the sequence of events from endothelial injury to an acute coronary occlusion by plaque rupture.
markingGuide: Endothelial dysfunction at sites of disturbed flow from risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes
LDL enters and is oxidised in the intima; monocytes become macrophages and form foam cells (fatty streak)
Smooth muscle migration and collagen deposition form fibrous cap over necrotic lipid core
Inflammation and enzyme degradation thin the cap; rupture exposes thrombogenic core
Platelet adhesion, aggregation and fibrin clot cause sudden luminal occlusion and acute coronary syndrome
questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory response to lipid in the vessel wall. Clinical events are caused by acute plaque rupture and thrombosis rather than by slow luminal narrowing alone.

questions.stem: Differentiate stable angina, unstable angina and myocardial infarction in terms of pathophysiology, ECG and troponin.
markingGuide: Stable angina: fixed stenosis, demand-driven ischaemia on exertion, relieved by rest, ECG normal at rest, troponin normal
Unstable angina: ruptured plaque with non-occlusive thrombus, rest or crescendo pain, troponin normal
Myocardial infarction: occlusive or prolonged ischaemia causing myocyte necrosis, troponin raised
STEMI: complete transmural occlusion with persistent ST elevation
NSTEMI: subendocardial necrosis with ST depression or T-wave change and raised troponin
questions.explanation: The three conditions lie on a continuum of ischaemia severity. Troponin distinguishes infarction from angina, and the ECG separates STEMI from NSTEMI.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man arrives one hour after severe chest pain began. His ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in V1-V4 and his first troponin is within the reference range. Interpret these findings, state which artery is likely involved, and explain why a normal troponin does not change management. Name two non-coronary conditions that can raise troponin.
markingGuide: ST elevation in V1-V4 indicates anterior transmural injury and STEMI
Likely culprit is the left anterior descending artery
Troponin lags necrosis by several hours so may be normal early
STEMI is a diagnosis made on clinical presentation and ECG; reperfusion should not wait for biomarkers
Troponin rise is not specific to coronary occlusion; examples are sepsis, pulmonary embolism, renal failure, myocarditis
questions.explanation: ST elevation reflects ongoing transmural ischaemia and is diagnostic in the right clinical setting. Troponin is a marker of necrosis that takes hours to appear, so early values may be normal and must not delay urgent treatment.
